We write as public health social scientists at Advancing New Standards in Reproductive Health (ANSIRH), in the Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology & Reproductive Sciences at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). At ANSIRH, we conduct innovative, rigorous, multidisciplinary research on complex issues related to sexual and reproductive health. 

We have analyzed the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) for Proposed Rule RIN 2900-AS31(P), and we oppose the rule on the basis of inadequate evidence and inaccurate assumptions used in the methodology for that RIA. Our analysis shows that the VA’s estimates on the effects of this proposed rule change on society are drastically underestimated. We comment on specific inadequate or inaccurate aspects of the analysis in our attached letter, which we submit as part of our official comment on this proposed rule. In the letter, we document (with cited evidence) several specific ways that the Impact Analysis of the Proposed Rule has dramatically failed to demonstrate an accurate assessment of the true financial and social costs of this proposed policy change. Thus, we call on the VA to conduct a more thorough and accurate impact assessment, and leave the existing rule in place so that it can continue to benefit U.S. veterans and family members.

September 2, 2025 
 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
Comment on Proposed Rule VA-2025-VHA-0073-0002, Reproductive Health Services 
 
To whom it may concern: 
 
We write as public health social scientists at Advancing New Standards in 
Reproductive Health (ANSIRH), in the Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology & 
Reproductive Sciences at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). At 
ANSIRH, we conduct innovative, rigorous, multidisciplinary research on complex 
issues related to sexual and reproductive health.  
 
We have analyzed the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) for Proposed Rule RIN 2900-
AS31(P), and we oppose the rule on the basis of inadequate evidence and inaccurate 
assumptions used in the methodology for that RIA. Our analysis shows that the VA’s 
estimates on the effects of this proposed rule change on society are drastically 
underestimated. We comment on specific inadequate or inaccurate aspects of the 
analysis below. 
 
1. Critically, the Regulatory Impact Analysis fails to take into account the well-
established body of rigorous evidence detailing the harms to pregnant people, 
children, and families when people cannot get the abortion care they need. Our 
landmark Turnaway Study followed nearly 1000 women over 5 years to document 
outcomes for those who were able to receive the abortion they sought compared to 
those who were denied care. The findings, published in over 100 peer-reviewed 
journal articles, show that being denied abortion care causes significant, lasting 
harms for women and their children.  
 
a. Pregnancy is physically risky, and carrying a pregnancy to term can lead to 
lasting physical health harms. Our research shows that women denied 
abortions are more likely to have serious health problems for years to come, 
compared to those who received the abortion care they sought. These lasting 
harms included chronic pain, hypertension, self-reported poor health, and 
even maternal death. The VA’s Impact Analysis itself acknowledges that the 
“veteran population using VA’s maternity benefit... is a population known to 
be at high risk for complications of pregnancy including severe maternal

 
2 | P a g e  
 
morbidity and pregnancy-associated death.” This suggests that the risks of physical harm from 
carrying a pregnancy to term would be even higher among the veteran population than 
among the general population of women in the Turnaway Study. Only the pregnant person 
can decide whether such risks are worth it.1,2  
 
b. Being denied abortion care is also associated with lasting negative economic status. Women 
who are denied abortions are more likely to experience financial hardship, including 
bankruptcies and debt, and to live in poverty, compared to those who receive the abortion 
they sought – even years later.3,4  
 
c. Finally, it is well known that the majority of people who seek abortion care are already 
mothers. When people cannot get the abortion care they need, the wellbeing of their existing 
children and future children is also negatively impacted, in significant, lasting ways. Our 
research shows that children whose mothers were denied an abortion are more likely to grow 
up in poverty and to miss their developmental milestones.5,6 
 
Thus the RIA’s Table 2, summarizing “Effects on Society” of this proposed rule, clearly fails to take into 
account the long-lasting effects on the people who will be unable to access abortion care as a result of this 
rule, as well as on their children. 
 
In the remainder of this comment, we address the inadequate methodology for the RIA analysis in Table 1, 
with specific critiques and citations from the peer-reviewed scientific literature. 
 
2. The Regulatory Impact Analysis assumes that about 60% of those who would seek abortions would 
ultimately obtain their abortions, with the rationale that 60% live in states where abortion is legal.   
However, legal does not mean accessible.  There are many states where abortion is legal but not 
accessible, including states like Georgia, Florida and Iowa with 6 week bans—a point at which many 
people do not even know they are pregnant.7  But even in states with few abortion restrictions, lack of 
providers and logistical and cost barriers prevent many people from being able to obtain the abortion 
they seek.8,9 Hence, there is no reason to believe that any VA abortion seekers would be able to obtain 
an abortion outside of the VA and CHAMPVA.  Evidence shows that costs are the greatest barrier to 
abortion care, frequently resulting in catastrophic expenditures.10–12 When people cannot pay for their 
abortions, they are commonly forced to carry the pregnancy to term.    
 
3. The Regulatory Impact Analysis uses outdated costs for the self-pay price for abortion, leading to 
underestimated costs. We know these costs are outdated because the RIA cites our own analysis,13 
and we have since published updated data on the costs of abortion, as recently as 2023.14 
Furthermore, self-pay costs (what clinics charge patients who are uninsured) are likely to be much 
lower than actual costs of providing the care. Thus, the Regulatory Impact Analysis’ estimates for the 
costs of abortion provision are likely systematically underestimated.  
 

3 | P a g e  
 
4. The Regulatory Impact Analysis projects that 50% of people seeking abortions will seek medication 
abortion and thus will not have to travel. This is not an accurate assumption. While the assumption 
that half would likely be medication abortions is likely accurate, many people who have medication 
abortions must still travel for care.  Residents of states with total abortion bans cannot legally access a 
prescription for mifepristone for abortion in their home state. Additionally, even in states where 
abortion is legal, providers can be scarce, and patients still have to travel long distances to reach an 
abortion clinic.  For example, hundreds of Wisconsin residents travel to Minnesota and Illinois each 
month because there are many more providers in those states.15  
 
5. No details are listed regarding assumptions of travel costs for people needing to seek abortion care 
beyond VA services. Actual studies of people traveling for abortion care have found a wide range of 
travel costs. One recent study found that travel times, costs, and delays for abortion care have all 
increased dramatically since the U.S. Supreme Court Dobbs decision. In particular, overnight stays 
have increased from 5% of traveling abortion care seekers to 58%, significantly increasing the costs of 
this travel. There is no indication that any of these data were referenced in the RIA methodology.16 
 
6. The proposed rule asserts that lifesaving procedures would still be performed under the medical 
benefits package. However, ANSIRH research shows that policies that ban abortion care can also lead 
to life-threatening delays and complications in many pregnancy care cases.17 In clinical settings where 
abortion is not allowed, obstetric care suffers for patients, including many who are not seeking 
abortion. Policies that ban abortion care have altered the standard of clinical care in a wide range of 
scenarios, including miscarriage management, in ways that contribute to delays, worsen health 
outcomes, and increase the cost and logistic complexity of care. In several cases ANSIRH research has 
documented, patients experienced preventable complications, such as severe infection or other life-
threatening crises, because clinicians reported their “hands were tied,” making it impossible for them 
to provide treatment sooner. 
 
7. The VA assumes that 50% of veteran enrollees would have relied on the VA for their maternity care if 
the abortion had not occurred. This is a fundamental assumption underlying the cost analysis, yet no 
support is provided for this assertion.  Thus, we are unable to assess the accuracy of this claim, or of 
any of the claimed estimates of total maternity care costs.  
 
8. The analysis estimates maternity and newborn costs including non-delivery costs which mostly 
consists of antepartum care, but does include some postpartum care. The analysis provides very 
limited details on what costs are included. The vague reference to “some postpartum care” is likely to 
be underestimated if the pregnant person or newborn experienced complications.  Thus, the analysis 
is likely to have underestimated costs associated with carrying an unwanted pregnancy to term. 
 
Given these points, it is clear that the Impact Analysis of the Proposed Rule has dramatically failed to 
demonstrate an accurate assessment of the true financial and social costs of this proposed policy change. 

4 | P a g e  
 
Thus, we call on the VA to conduct a more thorough and accurate impact assessment, and leave the 
existing rule in place so that it can continue to benefit U.S. veterans and family members.  
 
 
 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Katie Woodruff, DrPH 
Associate Professional Researcher 
Public Health Social Scientist 
 
 
 
Ushma Upadhyay, PhD, MPH 
Professor 
Public Health Social Scientist
